findings.passage: Dean, more often than not, lets the look take the hit.
findings.problem: The draft defines the Two/Three discriminator as what she protects 'when image and connection pull apart', but none of the evidence that follows involves a relationship at all. The examples (Messy title, 'wangled', 'depressive state', LA sessions 'went quite terribly', charts 'a dangerous game', deleting the apps) are candor about failure, each told after a success: 'wangled' in the same interview celebrating the Mercury nomination and followed by 'no, I'm supposed to be here'; the failed LA sessions told days before the hit album's release, as its origin story; the charts line ends 'But it feels great' (Music Week, re-opened 2026-10-23). Told-from-success failure is the shape of a Three's redemption narrative, and the draft itself concedes Messy 'is a brand'. The app deletion actually runs the other way: ELLE frames it as Dean being 'mindful not to let it impact her self-image', and she says 'I don't think you're supposed to know everyone's opinion about you' (S10, re-opened). That is protecting self-image, not letting it take a hit. So the stated discriminator is never observed, and 'more often than not' implies a count the article doesn't make.
findings.acceptance_test: The Three section either (a) cites at least one dated, sourced episode where keeping a relationship visibly cost her image or standing and she chose the relationship (one candidate to check is whether a source shows the Grammy speech's turn to her grandmother and immigrants carried image risk in the 2026 US climate), or (b) renames the discriminator to what the evidence shows (public candor about failure, told after success), says in one sentence that a Three's redemption narrative explains the same pattern, and lowers the weight of 'the record leans Two' to match. The app deletion is either dropped from the anti-Three list or given ELLE's self-image framing. 'More often than not' is removed unless image-vs-connection conflicts are actually counted.

findings.passage: The order is the detail. The apology to fans came first, the fight came second, and the fight was with companies her tours run through.
findings.problem: Every behavioral act offered for the Two motive costs little, gets rewarded by an audience, or follows a script. The champagne went to the writer of her cover story. The speech used an acceptance-speech convention. Twice she said sorry and then made it right (Ticketmaster, Auckland), which is the standard service-recovery and crisis-PR sequence any well-run artist team would follow. The draft admits that a Three would make the same moves and that 'Any headliner apologizes', and then still treats the sequence as a signature ('What matches November is the sequence'). Two scripted instances don't make a motive pattern. The standard's Enneagram-8 anchor needs repeated costly choices that the motive explains better than its rival. The record's costly choices (leaving Goldsmiths after three weeks, abandoning the LA sessions, keeping features off the album, deleting the apps at her peak, 'too scared to belong to anyone') mostly protect her autonomy and authorship, and the draft files them as counterevidence. Ticketmaster is the only episode with real cost: it publicly antagonized business partners. Even there, THR says her team may have set resale terms. The title thesis ('Handing the Moment Back') therefore rests on acts that don't separate Two from Three.
findings.acceptance_test: Either the article names at least one sourced, dated costly choice (money, career, standing or comfort) that the Two motive explains better than Three, or it states plainly that the Two behavioral evidence is low-cost, audience-visible conduct a Three would also show. The 'sequence' sentences either note that apology-then-remedy is the standard response or are cut, and the confidence language in the type answer, FAQ and 'the record leans Two' is adjusted to the weaker evidence.

findings.passage: After their interview ran long in a pub, Wilkinson wrote: "She's here to please."
findings.problem: The draft uses a 2023 journalist's characterization ('here to please') as Two-flavored support but leaves out Dean's own direct statements of independence from approval, all in S10, the source behind the hook, re-opened 2026-10-23. In ELLE 2026 she says: 'I know who I am, and I know that I'm performing and creating from a pure place. You can't please everybody. And I have such peace in that.' Also: 'My joy is more powerful than whatever you think about me or how I should be presenting.' This sentence directly precedes the 'I'll always choose joy' line the draft quotes, so the draft cut around it. On the apps: 'I don't think you're supposed to know everyone's opinion about you.' The Two's pride-in-being-needed and the heart-triad 'worth' reading both predict sensitivity to approval. These lines are the subject's own counterevidence on the exact axis the type argument depends on, so leaving them out tilts the case.
findings.acceptance_test: At least one of these ELLE 2026 lines ('You can't please everybody. And I have such peace in that.' or 'My joy is more powerful than whatever you think about me or how I should be presenting.') appears near the 'here to please' line or in the tension section, quoted in context. A sentence says how the Two read handles it: therapy-era self-description, a healthy Two, or counterevidence. The evidence record gains the matching claim(s) with S10.

findings.passage: Then there is a word she keeps using. Twice in the interviews gathered here, when she put herself first, she called it selfish.
findings.problem: This section presents her use of 'selfish' as a guilt reflex, evidence that her default is serving others. The Time Out instance (S03, re-opened 2026-10-23) says the opposite. The full passage reads: 'I learned that I know best, which can sound dickheaded... It's very easy to let other people tell you what you should be doing. But actually... you know immediately what you want to do. I learned that I had to be selfish. And make myself happy first. Who gives a fuck what other people think about it?' There 'selfish' is used approvingly, as a hard-won lesson in self-trust, ending in an explicit rejection of others' opinions. The draft stops the quote before 'Who gives a fuck what other people think about it?', and the cut sentence is the one that cuts against a Two. Only the British Library 'Carmen' use ('felt quite selfish at the time') carries a guilt tone. Two uses with opposite valence aren't 'a word she keeps using', and C44 sits in the type hypothesis's for_claim_ids on this misreading.
findings.acceptance_test: The Time Out line is extended through 'Who gives a fuck what other people think about it?' or paraphrased so its defiant tone is clear. 'A word she keeps using' and 'Twice... she called it selfish' are revised so the two uses are no longer presented as one guilt pattern. The 'songs belong to the listener' inference rests only on Carmen, the blurred covers and Numéro, with its limit stated. In evidence-draft, C44's inference is corrected and C44 is moved from for_claim_ids to the against case (or the move is justified).

findings.passage: Fear of danger would point to the head types, and anger to the gut types. Hers is a question of worth.
findings.problem: This triad step narrows the field to the heart types (2, 3, 4), and the gloss that heart-type shame is 'about being the wrong amount: too much, or not enough' looks tailored to fit 'too much'. Yet Four, the third heart type, is never named. The record has substantial Four-flavored material, some of it already in the draft: she moves toward intense vulnerability ('the best thing in the world'), says 'it's got to be my story', 'I need to be across all of it', 'I'm too scared to belong to anyone' and 'my heart has got a hard case'. Elsewhere in her sources: 'I've always held fast in what I know I'm good at, and that is expressing true, raw emotion and storytelling' and 'my own space that didn't have anyone else's impression on it' (Music Week 2025, re-opened); 'I felt quite different to everybody else' (Time Out 2023, re-opened). The draft even spends the 'steers toward pain' argument against Seven, which is itself Four evidence. The evidence record's own 'unexplained' and C35 name a Four streak, but the article never tests it. The anti-Three discriminator (candor over polish) doesn't separate Two from Four either.
findings.acceptance_test: A short passage near the Three comparison names Four and gives its best sourced evidence. Wherever the article uses 'I felt quite different to everybody else', it keeps the context that she was 'one of the only Black girls' at primary school, so circumstance isn't read as type. The passage then gives a sourced discriminator that survives it. Candidates already in the record: she left Goldsmiths because there 'you had to be making something really alternative and left to be cool' (Time Out 2023); 'instead of being negative... I'm trying to make it a positive' (Time Out 2023); 'I really don't have time to fester in negative emotions' (ELLE 2026); and blurred covers so listeners 'hear their own truth'. The 'wrong amount' gloss is either attributed as the author's reading or dropped.

findings.passage: And Sevens tend to steer away from pain. Dean steers toward it.
findings.problem: The anti-Seven verdict rests on songwriting vulnerability. Confessional writing is the genre's job, as the evidence record's C22 alternative notes, and she frames the vulnerability as a high: 'the best thing in the world'. The test also leaves out her own Seven-style reframing statements. In ELLE 2026 (S10, re-opened): 'I really don't have time to fester in negative emotions toward love and men. It doesn't serve me. I can be annoyed and hurt, but I try to find perspective and compassion.' In Time Out 2023 (S03, re-opened), on her mixed heritage: 'instead of being negative, which it was for me when I was younger, I'm trying to make it a positive.' Meanwhile the strongest Seven evidence sits in a different section and is weighed only against the Two stereotype, never against Seven: fear of being pinned ('I'm too scared to belong to anyone'), 'intensely romantic, but also no worries if not', love 'spread throughout your life rather than in one place', 'I've got to have as much fun as possible'. So the Seven case is presented weaker than the record makes it, and the discriminator chosen is the one most open to a genre explanation.
findings.acceptance_test: The Seven section quotes or paraphrases the ELLE 'fester' line or the Time Out 'make it a positive' line, and explicitly counts the freedom and no-belonging lines as Seven evidence. The verdict rests on a discriminator that survives them, or the section says Seven is not ruled out. A candidate already in the draft: her stated wish to stay in her comfort zone (Ward's recollection) and decade-long continuity with her manager and band, against a Seven's appetite for new options. 'Dean steers toward it' is qualified as songwriting and performing conduct.

findings.passage: Nines also tend to avoid open conflict. Dean took on three of the biggest companies in live music by name, on the same day the tickets went wrong.
findings.problem: This is the only discriminator offered against Nine, and it's weak. The confrontation was a set of Instagram stories posted on fans' behalf, which the evidence record (C29j alternative) itself calls lower-cost conflict. Speaking up for others is a well-known Nine pattern even when Nines won't fight for themselves. The Nine case also has more material than the draft weighs: 'quite a peaceful job' (Numéro), 'I really want to be in my comfort zone', 'You can't please everybody. And I have such peace in that' (ELLE 2026), deleting the apps to avoid knowing 'everyone's opinion about you'. The draft holds a much better anti-Nine discriminator elsewhere and doesn't use it here: her insistence on her own agenda and authorship ('it's got to be my story', 'I need to be across all of it', and Braham's 'both of us are very stubborn').
findings.acceptance_test: Nine is rejected on a discriminator that a Nine standing up for others wouldn't also satisfy, such as the authorship and stubbornness evidence. Otherwise the Ticketmaster sentence is qualified as a low-cost online statement made for fans, and the peace-language lines are acknowledged as the Nine's best evidence.

findings.passage: Her own definitions of purpose and success are about other people, and what reporters watched her do points the same way.
findings.problem: The plain-language answer directly under the type H2 states 'Olivia Dean's personality type is Enneagram Type 2' with no confidence level and no rival. The medium-confidence caveat and the Three rival arrive two paragraphs later. Yet the research record's drafting guidance asked for 'most likely' or 'reads as' language and for Three to be named inside the answer. This block is what search snippets lift, so it stands alone. 'What reporters watched her do' also overstates the observed record. Exactly one act was witnessed by a reporter and points this way: the ELLE champagne. 'Here to please' is a characterization, and the Ticketmaster and Auckland material is her own statements as reported. The standard says a later caveat does not license certainty elsewhere.
findings.acceptance_test: The answer of 60 words or fewer under '## What is Olivia Dean's personality type?' carries the confidence ('reads as' or 'most likely', medium confidence) and names Type 3 as the closest rival. 'What reporters watched her do' is replaced by wording that matches the record, such as 'what she did when her shows went wrong' or naming the specific episodes.

protected_passages.passage: Calling her boundary talk "Two growth" would make the theory impossible to lose. So it stays here as a tension the type does not resolve.
protected_passages.reason: A rare explicit refusal of the unfalsifiable 'growth/arrow' escape hatch. It keeps the type argument honest and should survive any rewrite of the tension section.

protected_passages.passage: The first sentence sounds like a Two. The second explains goodness by what it gets you.
protected_passages.reason: Reads one quote both ways instead of cherry-picking the half that fits. This is the model for how the fixes to the selfish and here-to-please passages should handle mixed evidence.

protected_passages.passage: The Two's usual costs, over-giving and resentment at going unthanked, do not show up in public. That could be health, privacy, or a sign the read is wrong.
protected_passages.reason: Names the missing shadow behavior that a Two read should predict and says plainly that the read could be wrong.

protected_passages.passage: When she describes what she wants from it, and from life off the road, listen for which she names: people and giving, goals and standing, freedom, or peace.
protected_passages.reason: A concrete, observable settle signal that separates the four live hypotheses by motive rather than by behavior. It is good for durability and for a future refresh.

protected_passages.passage: These are campaign answers for an album about love, and an album about love rewards them. "How many people you can gather in one space" is also a ticket count.
protected_passages.reason: The draft discounts its own best motive quote for professional incentive. That is exactly the motive-versus-incentive test this role looks for.

assessment: The draft avoids most typing traps. It uses no wings, arrows or subtypes to explain contradictions away. It refuses the 'Two growth' move by name, gives Three its own section with its best evidence, discounts campaign love-talk, and admits the Two's shadow costs are not in the record. The type argument still has no working discriminator. (1) The Two behavior that carries the title (birthday champagne for a cover-story writer, an acceptance speech, apology-then-remedy twice) is low-cost, audience-rewarded or scripted, and a Three would do all of it (enneagram-2). (2) The stated Two/Three discriminator, image versus connection, is never actually observed. Its evidence is candor about failure told from success, which a Three's redemption narrative also produces, and the app deletion was framed by ELLE as protecting her self-image (enneagram-1). The evidence also tilts by selection. Dean's own approval-independence statements in the hook source (ELLE 2026: 'You can't please everybody. And I have such peace in that'; 'My joy is more powerful than whatever you think about me') are left out while a writer's 'here to please' is used. The Time Out 'selfish' quote is cut before 'Who gives a fuck what other people think about it?', which reverses the meaning the section relies on (enneagram-3, enneagram-4). On the rest of the field: the heart-triad step admits Four, which is never tested (enneagram-5). The Seven test omits her 'no time to fester in negative emotions' reframing and never weighs the freedom lines against Seven (enneagram-6). The Nine rejection uses the weakest available discriminator (enneagram-7). The type answer drops the confidence and the rival (enneagram-8). Type 2 can remain a defensible leading read: the 'most useful' and 'how many people you can touch' self-definitions, the relational purpose statement and the Grammy and Carmen material are real. But medium confidence is the ceiling and isn't yet earned by a discriminator that survives Three, Four and Seven. If the fixes can't source a costly or image-versus-connection choice, the editor should state that limit in the body, the answer and the FAQ rather than keep 'the record leans Two' as written. Sources I re-opened on 2026-10-23 and matched against the draft and record: ELLE 2026 (S10), Time Out 2023 (S03) and Music Week 2025 (S22). YouTube sources were not re-transcribed, and 'quite aloof' and 'too empathetic can get you into trouble' in the S15 captions were not used because of speaker uncertainty. Similarity advisory: not tripped (max 0.125, against bill-clinton, on the generic sentence 'The Two's pattern runs in plain steps'). The arguments are not reused. Line 175 is the most textbook paragraph, and its claim that her songs 'keep circling' the Two's cost rests on one song plus an interview line. major_thesis_change is left false on purpose: if the resolution changes the leading type or replaces the central discriminator, it should hold for --refresh --expanded-review so the new argument gets independent challenge.
